name: Spanish Viridian
lede: Spanish Viridian is a deep blue-green named for the pigment viridian, a chromium oxide green whose other names the 1955 ISCC-NBS system filed decades before this particular qualifier existed.

sections.title: A viridian, by another name
sections.body:
Our library classes this as a pigment or dye word, built on viridian, the chromium oxide green pigment, though the word 'Spanish' itself is unexplained in the books we checked, and the name reads as one more obscure, qualified variant rather than a documented regional pigment [1]. The ISCC-NBS system's 1955 block for this exact hue carries several other filed names instead: Chrome Green, dated to 1815 in Maerz & Paul's 1930 dictionary, and Chromium Oxide, dated to 1838 — 'Spanish Viridian' itself is not among the names that dictionary filed [1].

Its real nearest look-alike is [[generic-viridian]], almost the same hue and treated in our graph as the color this name is also drawn from, with [[signal-green]] close behind, and [[amazon]] and [[tropical-rainforest]] a little further out, both duller [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this green in 10 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.04 percent, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 5 — rarer than 75 percent of the named colors we track [3]. The earliest match is from 1783, with the latest from 1940, eight dated paintings in all, a floor and not a first given how thin the archive's early centuries are [3].

origin.named_after: the pigment viridian (chromium oxide green); 'Spanish' itself is undocumented in our sources
